Momentum (p)

 Home Physics Branches of physics Classical mechanics
OurBigBook.com Words: 7k Articles: 63
For a nonrelativistic point mass of fixed mass m>0, measured in an inertial frame, its momentum is
p=mv.
(1)
Momentum is a vector pointing along the velocity, with International System of Units unit kgm/s. Doubling either mass or velocity doubles momentum. In one dimension, a chosen positive direction makes p=mv a signed quantity: a 2kg body moving right at 3m/s has p=+6kgm/s; moving left at the same speed gives p=−6kgm/s. [ref]
For a collection, total momentum is the vector sum P=∑i​mi​vi​. Two equal masses moving with opposite velocities can have zero total momentum while both have positive kinetic energy. Direction is therefore essential when using momentum conservation; adding speeds instead of signed velocities gives the wrong balance.
Newton's second law connects the net force on one fixed-mass point mass to its momentum through Fnet​=dp/dt. Integrating that change gives impulse. Here p denotes mechanical momentum; when canonical momentum differs from mass times velocity, the distinction in mechanical momentum below applies. The nonrelativistic formula also has a limited regime: special relativity is needed at speeds comparable with the speed of light.

Mechanical momentum (π=p−qA)

Words: 30
Momentum OurBigBook.com
For a charged particle minimally coupled to a magnetic vector potential, the mechanical momentum is π=p−qA, with p the canonical momentum. It is the mass times velocity in nonrelativistic mechanics.

Momentum conservation

Words: 398 Articles: 3
Momentum OurBigBook.com
Momentum conservation states that total momentum stays constant when the net force exerted from outside the chosen collection is zero. Use a closed collection, meaning the same fixed-mass point masses are followed throughout, and an inertial frame. Then
P=∑i​pi​,dtdP​=∑i​Fiext​.
(2)
To see why, sum Newton's second law over the members. If Fij​ is the force on member i from member j, Newton's third law assumes Fij​=−Fji​. Each pair cancels in the total:
dtdP​=∑i​Fiext​+∑i<j​(Fij​+Fji​)=∑i​Fiext​.
(3)
The internal forces act on different bodies and can change their individual momenta; their contributions cancel only in the collection's sum. An isolated system has no external interaction, but balanced external forces also suffice for momentum conservation. A closed system merely excluding matter exchange need not have conserved momentum. [ref]
The usefulness is that the detailed internal forces during a collision need not be known. Both an elastic collision and a perfectly inelastic collision obey the same isolated momentum balance; kinetic energy conservation is an additional condition for the elastic collision. If the external impulse is small but nonzero, the total momentum change is correspondingly small. For a variable-mass system exchanging matter, the entering or leaving momentum must also be included.
In a translation-invariant field theory, integrating over the spacetime zero mode enforces momentum conservation at interactions and scattering amplitudes.

Equal-mass fragmentation energy budget (ΔK=21​mw2)

Words: 70
Momentum conservation OurBigBook.com
If a mass m moving at u splits into equal fragments at velocities u±w, conservation of momentum fixes their centre-of-mass velocity. Their kinetic energy increases by mw2/2, independent of u. Thus an internal release energy Q gives w=2Q/m​. A front fragment must exceed a leading target's speed to close a pre-existing separation; merely matching speed does not intercept it. This kinematic result does not specify subsequent capture or braking.

For downward pre-ejection speed v0​, total mass M0​, payload mass mp​, and downward payload speed vp​ in the original inertial frame, the remaining body's upward speed is (mp​vp​−M0​v0​)/(M0​−mp​). Recoil (ER​≃p2/(2M))

Words: 78
Momentum conservation OurBigBook.com
Recoil is the motion acquired by a body when it exchanges momentum with an emitted, absorbed or scattered particle. For isolated emission from a body initially at rest, momentum conservation makes the remaining body acquire the opposite momentum. If its final mass is M and the recoil is nonrelativistic, its kinetic energy is ER​≃p2/(2M). A photon of energy Eγ​ has momentum magnitude Eγ​/c, so ER​≃Eγ2​/(2Mc2). The transition energy is shared between the photon and the recoiling body; nuclear recoil is an important example.

Rocket equation

Words: 2k Articles: 18
Momentum OurBigBook.com
The ideal rocket equation gives the change in signed velocity produced by ejecting rocket propellant. Assume one-dimensional Newtonian mechanics in an inertial frame, no external force, and a fixed positive rocket exhaust speed u directed rearward relative to the instantaneous rocket. The rocket's instantaneous mass M includes its remaining rocket propellant; burning it gives dM<0. For initial and final masses Minitial​≥Mfinal​>0,
Mdv=−udM,Δv=vfinal​−vinitial​=ulnMfinal​Minitial​​.
(4)
Here ln is the natural logarithm, and its argument is the rocket mass ratio. This is the constant-rocket exhaust speed, zero-pressure-correction version of the ideal rocket equation. [ref]
For a toy rocket with u=2km/s, Minitial​=1000kg and rocket dry mass Mfinal​=250kg after all rocket propellant is spent, the rocket mass ratio is 4 and
Δv=2ln4km/s≃2.7725887km/s.
(5)
Burning from 1000 to 500kg gains 2ln2km/s≃1.3863km/s. Burning from 500 to 250kg gains exactly the same velocity increment, using only 250kg of rocket propellant instead of 500kg. Both burns halve the remaining mass. The second burn accelerates a lighter rocket; equal fractional mass losses give equal velocity gains.
The natural logarithm makes the rocket equation both useful and revealing: multiplying successive rocket mass ratios adds their velocity gains. Conversely, the required rocket mass ratio is the exponential function Minitial​/Mfinal​=eΔv/u. Each extra uln2 of ideal velocity gain doubles the required initial mass for fixed final mass. This explains why a larger rocket exhaust speed is valuable and why carrying ever more rocket propellant has diminishing returns. Changing the burn duration alone does not change this ideal endpoint result.
For a short proof outline, follow the rocket together with a tiny parcel about to be expelled. Before ejection, their total momentum is Mv. After ejection, the remaining rocket has mass M+dM and velocity v+dv, while the parcel has positive mass −dM and, to first order, inertial velocity v−u. Momentum conservation gives
Mv=(M+dM)(v+dv)+(−dM)(v−u),0=Mdv+udM+dMdv.
(6)
Discarding the second-order product dMdv gives Mdv=−udM; taking the integral gives Δv=−u∫Minitial​Mfinal​​dM/M. Evaluating the integral yields the natural logarithm above. This is a variable-mass system calculation: the rocket alone is not a closed system, and its momentum changes as the expelled material carries away momentum. The fixed collection consisting of the rocket and all its expelled material has conserved total momentum when external forces vanish.
Fixed rocket exhaust speed means fixed relative speed at release, not fixed inertial velocity. As the rocket's velocity v changes, newly emitted material has changing inertial velocity v−u; previously released parcels coast at their own release velocities in this ideal model. If v>u, the exhaust even moves forward in the inertial frame, although it is emitted rearward relative to the rocket. No surrounding medium is needed for this exchange of momentum.
Real flight adds gravity, drag force and possibly a pressure correction to rocket thrust. A varying rocket thrust due solely to a changing mass loss rate still gives the same ideal rocket equation if u is constant; it changes the acceleration and burn duration. A changing rocket exhaust speed instead requires Δv=−∫udM/M, and external forces require their own contribution to the velocity change. The existing constant mass-loss propulsion with quadratic drag and constant-burn rocket with ground friction illustrate such additional forces; the forward-exhaust rocket equation reverses the ejection direction and therefore the sign of the recoil.

Rocket thrust (T=u(−M˙))

Words: 119
Rocket equation OurBigBook.com
Rocket thrust is the propulsive force associated with ejecting rocket propellant. In the ideal rocket equation with no pressure correction, T=u(−M˙), where M˙=dM/dt<0 is the signed rate of change of rocket mass and −M˙ is the positive mass loss rate. For u=2000m/s and M˙=−5kg/s, T=10000N. With no other force, the acceleration is T/M: initially 10m/s2 for M=1000kg, rising as mass falls if this rocket thrust stays constant.
A real exhaust outlet can also contribute a pressure term: T=u(−M˙)+Ae​(pe​−pa​), with exit area Ae​, exit pressure pe​ and ambient pressure pa​. The ideal formula here assumes that term vanishes; it must not silently absorb this correction while still interpreting u as the actual relative rocket exhaust speed. [ref]

Integration over a sliding interval gives v(t)−v(t0​)=ulog[q(t0​)/q(t)]−μg(t−t0​). From initial rest, immediate forward sliding additionally requires thrust to overcome static friction. u(t)=αQV​​tanh(QαV​​logm0​−Qtm0​​).

When matter leaves a moving body with zero instantaneous relative velocity, it carries the body's current momentum per unit mass but creates no additional recoil term. Dust-collecting rocket (mv˙=αu−βv2)

Words: 333 Articles: 3
Rocket equation OurBigBook.com
A classical rocket ejecting fuel at rate α>0 and relative exhaust speed u>0, while collecting stationary dust of mass βdx per traveled distance, obeys
m˙=βv−α,mv˙=αu−βv2.
(8)
These are mass conservation and momentum conservation for the rocket, incoming dust and outgoing gas. The dust-loading term supplies the momentum needed to accelerate incoming stationary material. Put λ=α/(βu)​ and V=λu. While the engines operate and 0≤v<V, an initially stationary rocket satisfies
m0​m​=(VV−v​)(λ−1)/2(VV+v​)−(λ+1)/2.
(9)
For λ>1, continuing to V would drive total mass to zero. For 0<λ<1, total mass instead grows without bound and V is approached only after infinite time under indefinitely maintained thrust. In both cases a finite fuel supply runs out before that limiting speed. Total stored mass must not be confused with remaining fuel.

Angular momentum (L=r×p)

Words: 5k Articles: 37
Momentum OurBigBook.com
Angular momentum measures how a point mass's momentum passes around a chosen origin. Motion straight toward or away from that origin contributes zero; transverse momentum contributes more when it passes farther away. The picture shows the sign convention before the calculation.
Fix an origin O and nonrotating axes in an inertial frame. For a nonrelativistic point mass of constant mass m>0, let r be its position from O and p=mv its mechanical momentum in that same reference frame. Its angular momentum is the cross product
LO​=r×p,∣LO​∣=rpsinϕ.
(11)
Here r=∣r∣, p=∣p∣, and ϕ∈[0,π] is the angle between them. The right-hand rule gives the direction: curl from r toward p, and the thumb points along LO​. Thus angular momentum is an axial vector, perpendicular to both position and momentum. Its International System of Units unit is kgm2/s. A point mass need not follow a circle to have angular momentum.[ref]
With x rightward, y upward, and +z out of the page, the cross product gives Lz​=xpy​−ypx​. Take
r=(2,0,0)m,p=(0,3,0)kgm/s.
(12)
Then LO​=(0,0,6)kgm2/s. Reversing the momentum makes Lz​=−6kgm2/s; radial momentum p=(3,0,0)kgm/s gives LO​=0. The factor rsinϕ is the lever arm to the line through the particle parallel to its momentum.
For motion in the xy plane, plane polar coordinates give v=r˙r+rθ˙θ, with r×θ=z. Consequently
Lz​=mr2θ˙,r2θ˙=mLz​​.
(13)
The signed angular velocity θ˙ is positive counterclockwise viewed from +z toward the plane, with θ measured in radians. Radial velocity does not enter the cross product. Under conservation of angular momentum, this relation predicts faster angular motion at smaller r and constant areal velocity A˙=Lz​/(2m) for consistently oriented swept area. That is the geometric content of Kepler's second law.
For several point masses, add their angular momenta about the same origin: LO​=∑i​ri​×pi​. The origin matters: angular momentum under an origin shift explains why the same moving particle can have different values about two fixed points. The central axis of a momentum system and angular momentum decomposition about the centre of mass make this dependence useful.

Angular momentum OurBigBook.com
Move the fixed origin from O to O′=O+a, keeping the axes parallel and the inertial frame's velocity measurements unchanged. The new positions are ri′​=ri​−a, so distributivity of the cross product gives
LO′​=∑i​(ri​−a)×pi​=LO​−a×P,P=∑i​pi​.

Here P is total linear momentum. For the angular momentum example with a=(1,0,0)m, the new position is (1,0,0)m and LO′,z​=6−3=3kgm2/s. A moving origin additionally contributes −a˙×P when this expression is differentiated while retaining the original momenta; see angular momentum about the centre of mass for an important case where that term vanishes.

Gyroscope

Words: 2k Articles: 8
Angular momentum OurBigBook.com
A gyroscope is a rotating instrument whose rapidly spinning, nearly symmetric rotor provides a direction reference through its angular momentum. In an inertial frame, negligible external torque approximately preserves that direction by conservation of angular momentum. A transverse torque turns the angular momentum instead: the surprising sideways motion of a supported spinning wheel is precession. An ideal freely falling test gyroscope in general relativity has its spin undergo parallel transport along its timelike geodesic. Comparing that direction with distant reference axes measures Lense-Thirring precession; the direction need not remain fixed in arbitrary rotating coordinates.
A gyroscope direction reference is useful precisely because its direction can persist while its housing turns. A spinning-wheel precession experiment deliberately supplies gravitational torque to reveal how that persistence fails. The gyroscope vector geometry explains the direction, and slow steady gyroscope precession gives a numerical prediction with a check on its assumptions.

Gyroscope OurBigBook.com
A flywheel's spin angular momentum Lf​ must turn with the vehicle. The vehicle supplies torque Ω×Lf​ to maintain this precession, and experiences the opposite reaction torque. With right-handed axes x forward, y left and z up, a left turn has Ω=+Ωz. A transverse flywheel with Lf​=−Lf​y​ then produces body torque −ΩLf​x, opposing outward roll. Its magnitude is Lf​v/Rb​ for turn radius Rb​. Reversing the flywheel reverses the effect.

Gyrocompass

Gyroscope OurBigBook.com
A gyrocompass uses a spinning gyroscope and Earth's rotation to identify geographical north. In an ideal model whose axle is constrained to the local horizontal plane but free to turn about the vertical, the northward direction of the spin angular momentum is stable away from the poles; the opposite spin direction is unstable. A real settling instrument also requires damping. This is different from merely preserving an initial inertial orientation with a freely mounted gyroscope.
Gyrocompass oscillation (ω02​=(I1​/I2​)ωΩE​cosλ)
Words: 89
Gyrocompass OurBigBook.com
For a rapidly spinning gyrocompass with axle constrained horizontally, take azimuth θ positive from north towards west and positive spin angular momentum Js​=I1​ω. In the terrestrial rotating reference frame, the vertical component of the torque equation, with zero external vertical torque, is I2​θ¨+Js​ΩE​cosλsinθ≃0. Here I2​ is the vertical moment of inertia and terms of order ΩE2​ have been neglected. The small-angle approximation about θ=0 gives simple harmonic motion with the displayed squared angular frequency. Linearizing about θ=π reverses its sign and gives an unstable equilibrium. At the poles this restoring effect vanishes. For a thin rotationally symmetric flywheel, the perpendicular axis theorem gives I1​=2I2​.

Gyroscope vector geometry (τO​=dLO​/dt)

Words: 290
Gyroscope OurBigBook.com
Choose a fixed support point O and nonrotating axes in an inertial frame. All angular momenta, torques, and moments of inertia below refer to O. Let e point along the axle from O toward the centre of mass, and let z point vertically upward. Write θ for their angle. For a rapidly spinning symmetric top, the dominant angular momentum is LO​≃Ls​e, where Ls​=I3​ω3​ is signed and I3​ is the axial principal moment of inertia. The sign of the axial angular velocity ω3​ follows the right-hand rule.
With mass M, centre of mass distance d, and constant gravitational acceleration g, the gravitational force and its torque are
r=de,Fg​=−Mgz,τO​=r×Fg​=Mgdz×e.
(15)
An ideal support applies a force at O, so its lever arm and torque about O vanish. At the instant the axle lies in the xz plane with a positive x component, the gravitational torque points along +y. It adds dLO​=τO​dt toward +y, rather than along the downward force. The dot product identity d∣LO​∣2/dt=2LO​⋅τO​ shows why perpendicular torque changes direction without instantly changing magnitude. This vector balance and the slow-turning relation τO​=Ω×LO​ are developed in Chapter 20: Rotation in space (sections 20-2 and 20-3, equations 20.13–20.15).
For steady precession about the vertical, Ω=Ωz and de/dt=Ωz×e. Equating the two cross products gives
Ω≃Ls​Mgd​=I3​ω3​Mgd​,∣τO​∣=Mgdsinθ.
(16)
The angular momentum tip traces a circle of radius ∣Ls​∣sinθ: its sideways speed is ∣ΩLs​∣sinθ. Both that radius and the gravitational lever arm contain sinθ, explaining its cancellation for 0<θ<π. Exactly vertical alignment has zero gravitational torque and no distinguishable azimuthal precession to infer by this cancellation. Positive Ls​ gives positive precession, counterclockwise viewed from above; reversing the spin reverses the slow precession. [ref]

Spinning-wheel precession experiment

Words: 472
Gyroscope OurBigBook.com
Purdue's Bicycle Wheel Gyroscope demonstration uses a bicycle wheel on a long axle, with a ball at one end seated in a freely rotating socket on a heavy stand. Spin the wheel by hand or with the supplied motor, seat the ball, and release the nearly horizontal axle. The readout is the axle sweeping around the vertical while the wheel continues spinning. Compare with the stopped wheel, which falls when one end is released; reverse the spin with the same support and the precession reverses. These are the page's documented apparatus, presentation, and reversal checks. [ref]
An alternative in Physics Demonstrations by Julien Clinton Sprott (section 1.3, Materials and Procedure) suspends one axle end by stainless steel wire and a fishing-line swivel. The swivel allows precession without winding up the suspension. Sprott describes the axle bobbing as nutation and precession becoming faster as spin decreases. A suspended support can move, whereas the calculation here assumes a fixed O; use the socket version for the closest realization. [ref]
A proposed quantitative extension is to record an overhead view of an axle marker against a fixed angle scale, together with a side view for θ(t). Time successive overhead passages to estimate Ω=2π/T; count passages of a rim mark to estimate ∣ω3​∣=2πf. Record the spin sense too. Measure M and the centre of mass offset d of the whole moving assembly, and determine its axial moment of inertia I3​ independently. Wheel, axle, support, release angle, and observation interval should stay the same between spin trials. Measuring both Ω and θ(t) distinguishes azimuthal precession from nutation; an overhead movie alone can miss the latter. These camera readouts and parameter checks are proposed here, not reported measurements from the demonstration pages.
For slow precession, compare ΩI3​ω3​ with Mgd, and test whether reversing ω3​ reverses Ω with nearly unchanged magnitude. A brief interval minimizes spin loss from friction; repeat at several starting spin rates rather than interpreting an entire slowing run as one steady state. A suspension restoring torque governed by its torsion constant, socket friction, support motion, a misplaced centre of mass, and a push at release can all supply extra torque or change the initial conditions. The swivel reduces the twist that activates the suspension's torsion constant; it does not demonstrate zero torque.
Steady precession keeps θ constant; nutation changes θ while the axle may also precess. Sudden release generally excites both. A small initial drop is consistent with conservation of energy and conserved vertical angular momentum: some gravitational potential energy supplies the motion around the vertical, and the axial contribution to vertical angular momentum adjusts. Bearing friction may damp the bobbing, but an ideal undamped heavy symmetric top need not settle into steady precession. Chapter 20: Rotation in space explicitly distinguishes uniform precession from release transients and nutation (section 20-3, paragraphs following equation 20.15).[ref]

Conservation of angular momentum (dLO​/dt=τOext​=0)

Angular momentum OurBigBook.com
Conservation of angular momentum says that total angular momentum stays fixed when the net external torque about the chosen fixed inertial origin vanishes. Individual angular momenta and angular velocities can change. The radius change at constant angular momentum below makes this distinction visible: pulling two rotating point masses inward lowers the moment of inertia, raises the angular velocity, and supplies work that increases the kinetic energy.
Follow the same constant-mass point masses throughout, in an inertial frame, with all positions measured from a fixed origin O. If the internal pair forces are opposite and central, meaning directed along each pair's separation, then
LO​=∑i​ri​×pi​,dtdLO​​=τOext​=∑i​ri​×Fiext​.
(24)
Thus zero net external torque throughout an interval implies constant total angular momentum throughout that interval. A vanishing external torque component, such as τzext​=0, conserves the corresponding Lz​ even when the other components change. This is the balance law for a fixed collection; angular-momentum flux must also be accounted for when matter crosses its boundary. [ref]
The central qualification is essential. Write Fij​ for the internal force on member i from member j. Under Newton's third law, Fji​=−Fij​, but the sum of their torques is
ri​×Fij​+rj​×Fji​=(ri​−rj​)×Fij​.
(25)
This vanishes when Fij​ is parallel to ri​−rj​. Equal-and-opposite forces alone do not suffice: two opposite transverse forces with separated lines of action form a couple with nonzero torque. Cancellation of the internal pair torques, together with Newton's second law, proves the total balance above.
For one point mass under a central force about O, F=f(r)r gives τO​=r×F=0. The force may still change the speed and kinetic energy; its zero torque preserves angular momentum. With nonzero LO​, r⋅LO​=0 keeps the motion in a fixed plane. Choosing the z axis perpendicular to that plane, r2θ˙=Lz​/m governs its angular progress. This removes an unknown from the central-force radial turning point calculation and helps reduce the Kepler orbit to a radial problem.
There is a historical geometric version of this result. In Book I, Section II, Proposition I of the Principia, Newton proves that motion under a central force toward a fixed centre stays in a plane and sweeps equal areas in equal times, using successive central impulses and equal triangle areas. [ref] In the modern notation above, constant areal velocity is A˙=Lz​/(2m): the old geometric proof and the angular momentum calculation express the same invariant.

Angular momentum OurBigBook.com
Torque measures a force's turning effect about a specified origin. The geometry in the angular momentum diagram applies with force replacing momentum: transverse forces give positive or negative torque, while a radial force gives zero. A longer perpendicular lever arm makes the same force more effective, explaining why pushing near the end of a handle is useful.
For a force F applied at position r from a fixed origin O in an inertial frame, its torque, or moment of force, is
τO​=r×F,∣τO​∣=rFsinϕ=Fℓ.
(30)
Here F=∣F∣, ϕ is the angle between position and force, and ℓ=rsinϕ is the perpendicular lever arm. Direction follows the right-hand rule; in the xy plane τz​=xFy​−yFx​, positive counterclockwise as viewed from +z. The International System of Units unit is Nm=kgm2/s2. Although torque and energy have the same physical dimensions, torque is an axial vector and energy is a scalar; their roles differ.
For r=(2,0,0)m and F=(0,3,0)N, τz​=+6Nm. Applying the same force at (1,0,0)m gives +3Nm; reversing it gives a negative torque; directing it along r gives zero. More generally, sum ri​×Fi​ to find the total torque about one common origin.
For a constant-mass point mass, the product rule and Newton's second law show why net torque changes angular momentum:
dtdLO​​=v×(mv)+r×dtdp​=r×Fnet​=τOnet​.
(31)
The first cross product vanishes because its factors are parallel. For a collection with canceling internal torques, the remaining sum is external torque, giving conservation of angular momentum when it vanishes.[ref]
A nonzero torque can turn the direction of angular momentum as well as change its magnitude. Indeed, the dot product gives d∣LO​∣2/dt=2LO​⋅τO​: a perpendicular torque changes direction without instantaneously changing the magnitude. This is the geometry behind gyroscope precession. For a rapidly spinning symmetric top with a fixed tip, centre of mass distance d from the tip, mass M, and spin-dominated angular momentum magnitude L≃Iω, the slow steady precession approximation gives Ω≃Mgd/L, where g is gravitational acceleration. [ref] This is an approximation with Ω≪ω; the uniform precession of a heavy symmetric top retains contributions omitted by the spin-dominated estimate.

Areal velocity measures how fast a position vector from a chosen origin sweeps signed swept area. In positively oriented Cartesian coordinates in the plane, and in plane polar coordinates with angle θ in radians,

for a constant mass m. If n is chosen along a nonzero conserved specific angular momentum vector, then hn​=h=∣r×v∣ and the familiar positive formula is A˙=h/2. Reversing the orientation changes the sign; the instantaneous unsigned swept-area rate is ∣A˙∣.

Orbital observations behind the area law

Words: 289 Articles: 2
Areal velocity OurBigBook.com
Why infer an area law from astronomy? In the authored account The great Martian catastrophe and how Kepler fixed it by Owen Gingerich, a 13 August 1593 Mars observation has ecliptic longitude 346∘7.5′, against predicted 342∘0′ and 351∘26′. These are Earth-based directions with a date, not measured Sun-based areas. The observer's armillary sphere used graduated circles and sighting arms to read declination; reversing it allowed a second reading. Comparing stars at different altitudes exposed refraction, and a planet-based check revealed an erroneous solar correction table. The apparent Mars distance signal had been contaminated by that correction. Johannes Kepler subsequently corrected the observer's Earth orbit, then tested Mars trajectories. The account describes typical angular errors of 2′ or less (120 arcseconds): small residuals needed care.[ref]
The Tufts class notes Kepler's Astronomia Nova and the Orbit of Mars explain the key limitation: an area requires a trajectory and distances, so Kepler's second law cannot be directly tested from angular observations alone. They describe checking the combined ellipse and area law against 28 dated observations around seven oppositions during 1583-1595, using an Earth model to predict Earth-based directions; agreement improved greatly but some discrepancies remained.[ref]
The inferential chain is useful today too: recover relative positions and times, compare swept areas, and ask what forces are compatible with their evolution. Agreement with equal areas supports zero torque about the chosen origin under the assumptions below; it alone does not identify an inverse-square law. Recovering the radial force also needs the trajectory and its timing, as in inferring an inverse-square force from Kepler laws. The two diagrams here are calculated examples, not the historical measurements.

The converse needs the fixed-plane assumption: a constant projected areal velocity in three dimensions only constrains one torque component. Also, r=0 makes the instantaneous torque vanish regardless of force and makes plane polar coordinates singular. A moving origin or changing plane requires additional terms.
